questions.title: Practical Task: Subtractive Synthesis Signal Flow
questions.content: Order the modules of a subtractive synthesiser from START (top) to OUTPUT (bottom).
items: Voltage Controlled Filter (VCF - Timbre & Cutoff Sculpting)
Voltage Controlled Oscillator (VCO - Raw Waveform Generation)
ADSR Envelope Generator (Modulates Filter Cutoff & Volume)
correct_order: Voltage Controlled Oscillator (VCO - Raw Waveform Generation)
Voltage Controlled Filter (VCF - Timbre & Cutoff Sculpting)
ADSR Envelope Generator (Modulates Filter Cutoff & Volume)
questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: In subtractive synthesis, the oscillator (VCO) creates a harmonically rich raw wave, the filter (VCF) removes unwanted frequencies, and the amplifier (VCA) shapes the final volume.

expert_quote.text: Subtractive synthesis is like sculpting marble. The oscillator provides the solid block of stone, and the filter carves away everything that isn't the sculpture.
expert_quote.author: Bob Moog, Synthesizer Pioneer

questions.expert_explanation: In subtractive synthesis, the oscillator (VCO) creates a harmonically rich raw wave, the filter (VCF) removes unwanted frequencies, and the amplifier (VCA) shapes the final volume.

explanation_image.alt: Practical Task: Subtractive Synthesis Signal Flow

questions.title: Practical Listening: Pure Fundamental Waveform
questions.content: Listen to the synthesiser tone and pick the pure waveform with NO harmonic overtones.
questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: A sine wave contains only the fundamental frequency with zero harmonic overtones, making it ideal for clean sub-bass layers.

expert_quote.text: A pure sine wave is the atom of all musical sound. Combine enough of them at differing amplitudes and phases, and you can reconstruct any acoustic instrument.
expert_quote.author: Jean-Baptiste Fourier

questions.expert_explanation: A sine wave contains only the fundamental frequency with zero harmonic overtones, making it ideal for clean sub-bass layers.

questions.title: Q3: Purpose of a Synthesiser Filter
questions.content: What is the main job of a filter (VCF) in a subtractive synthesiser?

answers.text: Add stereo delay and room reverb

questions.expert_explanation: A Voltage Controlled Filter (VCF) sculpts a synth's tone by cutting away frequencies from a bright raw waveform. Sweeping its cutoff turns a harsh sawtooth into a warm pad or bass.

expert_quote.text: The filter defines the sonic identity of a synthesizer.
expert_quote.author: Sound Synthesis Principles

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: A Voltage Controlled Filter (VCF) sculpts a synth's tone by cutting away frequencies from a bright raw waveform. Sweeping its cutoff turns a harsh sawtooth into a warm pad or bass.

explanation_image.alt: Q3: Purpose of a Synthesiser Filter

questions.title: Q4: ADSR Envelope Stages
questions.content: In an ADSR envelope, which stages control time and which controls level?

answers.text: Attack and Sustain are resonance; Decay is pitch
Attack and Decay are panning; Release is tone
All four stages control oscillator playback speed
Attack, Decay, Release are time; Sustain is level

questions.expert_explanation: Attack, Decay, and Release are measured in time (milliseconds or seconds), while Sustain is a held volume or cutoff level. Knowing this distinction is a classic Edexcel exam mark.

expert_quote.text: Remember: you set how long the attack, decay, and release take, but sustain is the volume the note rests at while your finger stays on the key.
expert_quote.author: Sound on Sound Synth Secrets

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Attack, Decay, and Release are measured in time (milliseconds or seconds), while Sustain is a held volume or cutoff level. Knowing this distinction is a classic Edexcel exam mark.

questions.title: Q5: Low-Pass Filter (LPF)
questions.content: What does a Low-Pass Filter (LPF) do to a synthesiser sound?

answers.text: Lets lows pass and cuts highs
Lets highs pass and cuts lows
Lets mids pass and cuts lows and highs
Cuts one narrow middle frequency band

questions.expert_explanation: A Low-Pass Filter lets frequencies below the cutoff point pass through while attenuating higher harmonics. Lowering the cutoff makes a bright synth sound warmer and darker.

expert_quote.text: Subtractive synthesis is the art of acoustic sculpture—the oscillator provides the raw block of marble, and the low-pass filter chisels away the excess brightness.
expert_quote.author: Bob Moog

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: A Low-Pass Filter lets frequencies below the cutoff point pass through while attenuating higher harmonics. Lowering the cutoff makes a bright synth sound warmer and darker.

questions.title: Q6: High-Pass vs Band-Pass Filters
questions.content: How does a High-Pass Filter (HPF) differ from a Band-Pass Filter (BPF)?

answers.text: HPF cuts highs; BPF boosts sub-bass only
HPF is digital only; BPF is analogue only
HPF cuts lows; BPF cuts both lows and highs
HPF raises pitch; BPF lowers pitch an octave

questions.expert_explanation: An HPF removes low rumble below the cutoff, while a BPF cuts both lows and highs to leave only a middle band. BPFs are great for thin, radio-style synth leads.

expert_quote.text: Use a high-pass filter to clean the mud out of your synths, and a band-pass filter when you want your lead to cut through the mix like a nasal telephone.
expert_quote.author: Sound on Sound Synth Secrets

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: An HPF removes low rumble below the cutoff, while a BPF cuts both lows and highs to leave only a middle band. BPFs are great for thin, radio-style synth leads.

questions.title: Q7: Filter Resonance (Q)
questions.content: What does turning up Filter Resonance (Q) do to the sound?

answers.text: Cuts all high frequencies for a dark tone
Boosts frequencies right at the cutoff point
Detunes two oscillators for a chorus effect
Shifts the note pitch up by one full octave

questions.expert_explanation: Resonance (Q) feeds part of the filter output back in to boost a sharp peak right at the cutoff frequency. Sweeping a resonant filter creates classic squelchy acid and synth leads.

expert_quote.text: Resonance is what turns a polite low-pass filter into a biting, screaming animal—feed the cutoff back on itself and the synth begins to sing.
expert_quote.author: Dave Smith

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Resonance (Q) feeds part of the filter output back in to boost a sharp peak right at the cutoff frequency. Sweeping a resonant filter creates classic squelchy acid and synth leads.

questions.title: Q8: Analogue Synth Oscillators (VCO)
questions.content: What does the acronym VCO stand for on an analogue synthesiser?
questions.expert_explanation: A Voltage Controlled Oscillator (VCO) generates the synth's raw starting waveform, with its pitch controlled by electrical voltage. Pressing higher keys sends a higher voltage to raise the pitch.

expert_quote.text: The VCO is where synthetic sound is born—a continuous stream of raw electrical oscillation shaped entirely by voltage.
expert_quote.author: Bob Moog

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: A Voltage Controlled Oscillator (VCO) generates the synth's raw starting waveform, with its pitch controlled by electrical voltage. Pressing higher keys sends a higher voltage to raise the pitch.

questions.title: Q9: LFO Pitch Modulation
questions.content: Routing a Low Frequency Oscillator (LFO) to oscillator pitch creates which effect?
questions.expert_explanation: An LFO cycles slowly below human hearing (0.1–20 Hz) to modulate other controls automatically. Routing an LFO to pitch produces vibrato, whereas routing it to volume (VCA) produces tremolo.

expert_quote.text: An LFO breathes life and motion into static synth patches—turning flat tones into expressive vibrato, pulsing tremolo, or evolving textures.
expert_quote.author: Sound on Sound Synth Secrets

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: An LFO cycles slowly below human hearing (0.1–20 Hz) to modulate other controls automatically. Routing an LFO to pitch produces vibrato, whereas routing it to volume (VCA) produces tremolo.

questions.title: Q10: Filter Envelope (EG to VCF)
questions.content: What happens when you route an Envelope Generator to the filter cutoff?

answers.text: It fades the master stereo volume up and down
It bends oscillator pitch into a divebomb
It opens and closes brightness over time
It morphs a sine wave into a square wave

questions.expert_explanation: Routing an envelope to the filter cutoff makes brightness change automatically as each note plays. Fast decay creates punchy synth plucks, while slow attack creates swelling brass pads.

expert_quote.text: Modulating the filter cutoff with an envelope is how we breathe acoustic life into static analog oscillators—turning a plain buzz into a biting bass or an expressive brass swell.
expert_quote.author: Bob Moog

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Routing an envelope to the filter cutoff makes brightness change automatically as each note plays. Fast decay creates punchy synth plucks, while slow attack creates swelling brass pads.

items.title: Topic 3: Synthesis (Part 2)
items.description: Mastery quiz covering the fundamentals of Synthesis.

questions.title: Q11: Pulse vs Square Wave Timbre
questions.content: How does a narrow pulse wave sound compared to a standard square wave?

answers.text: Smooth and warm vs harsh and aggressive
Only odd harmonics vs every harmonic
One octave lower vs one octave higher
Thin and nasal vs hollow and woody

questions.expert_explanation: A 50% square wave contains only odd harmonics, giving a hollow, woody tone. Narrowing the pulse width introduces even harmonics for a thinner, nasal, reedy sound.

expert_quote.text: A square wave gives you the hollow woody tones of a clarinet; narrowing that pulse introduces even harmonics that buzz with the nasal bite of an oboe.
expert_quote.author: Sound on Sound Synth Secrets

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: A 50% square wave contains only odd harmonics, giving a hollow, woody tone. Narrowing the pulse width introduces even harmonics for a thinner, nasal, reedy sound.

explanation_image.alt: Q11: Pulse vs Square Wave Timbre

questions.title: Practical Listening: Bright Harmonic Waveform
questions.content: Listen to the synthesiser tone and pick the bright, buzzy waveform containing both odd and even harmonics.
questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: A sawtooth wave contains every integer harmonic (both odd and even), creating a bright, buzzy sound ideal for synth brass, strings, and leads.

expert_quote.text: For fat lead sounds, synth brass, and classic analogue bass, the sawtooth wave remains the undisputed king of subtractive synthesis.
expert_quote.author: Dave Smith, Designer of the Prophet-5 & Co-Creator of MIDI

questions.expert_explanation: A sawtooth wave contains every integer harmonic (both odd and even), creating a bright, buzzy sound ideal for synth brass, strings, and leads.

questions.title: Q13: Filter Slopes (12 dB vs 24 dB)
questions.content: How does a 24 dB/octave filter differ from a 12 dB/octave filter?

answers.text: 24 dB has a steeper, sharper frequency cut
24 dB has a gentler, softer frequency roll-off
24 dB is digital only; 12 dB is analogue only
24 dB boosts bass; 12 dB cuts high frequencies

questions.expert_explanation: A 24 dB/octave (4-pole) filter cuts frequencies above the cutoff twice as steeply as a 12 dB/octave (2-pole) filter, giving a tighter, punchier bass response.

expert_quote.text: The 24dB-per-octave ladder filter is the heart of the Moog sound—it clamps down hard on upper harmonics to give synth bass that unmistakable weight and authority.
expert_quote.author: Bob Moog

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: A 24 dB/octave (4-pole) filter cuts frequencies above the cutoff twice as steeply as a 12 dB/octave (2-pole) filter, giving a tighter, punchier bass response.

explanation_image.alt: Q13: Filter Slopes (12 dB vs 24 dB)

questions.title: Q14: Granular Synthesis Principles
questions.content: How does granular synthesis manipulate recorded audio?

answers.text: Inverts phase to cancel background noise
Splits audio into tiny grains to stretch or freeze
Converts incoming audio directly into MIDI notes
Limits playback strictly to basic square waves

questions.expert_explanation: Granular synthesis slices a sample into tiny micro-grains (10–100 ms) that can be time-stretched, pitch-shifted, or frozen into evolving ambient pads.

expert_quote.text: Granular synthesis divorces time from pitch—transforming any brief sonic moment into an infinite, evolving landscape.
expert_quote.author: Curtis Roads

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Granular synthesis slices a sample into tiny micro-grains (10–100 ms) that can be time-stretched, pitch-shifted, or frozen into evolving ambient pads.

questions.title: Q15: Oscillator Hard Sync
questions.content: What happens when you use oscillator hard sync on a synthesiser?

answers.text: Two oscillators detune slightly for chorus
Oscillators lock strictly to the DAW tempo
One oscillator resets another, adding sharp harmonics
One oscillator adds slow pitch vibrato

questions.expert_explanation: In hard sync, a master oscillator forces a slave oscillator to restart its cycle every time the master repeats. Sweeping the slave pitch creates classic tearing, metallic synth leads.

expert_quote.text: Hard sync forces one oscillator to bow to another—yielding sharp, tearing harmonic sweeps that slice through any mix.
expert_quote.author: Dave Smith

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: In hard sync, a master oscillator forces a slave oscillator to restart its cycle every time the master repeats. Sweeping the slave pitch creates classic tearing, metallic synth leads.

questions.title: Q16: Additive Synthesis Examples
questions.content: Which classic instrument creates its tone using additive synthesis (layering sine waves)?
questions.expert_explanation: A Hammond organ uses nine drawbars to blend individual sine-wave harmonics together — a classic hardware example of additive synthesis.

expert_quote.text: Every drawbar on a Hammond organ is an acoustic dial for a sine wave partial—the earliest hands-on additive synthesiser in music history.
expert_quote.author: Sound on Sound Synth Secrets

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: A Hammond organ uses nine drawbars to blend individual sine-wave harmonics together — a classic hardware example of additive synthesis.

questions.title: Q17: VCO vs DCO Tuning Difference
questions.content: What is the main difference in tuning stability between a VCO and a DCO?

answers.text: VCOs drift with heat; DCOs stay digitally locked
VCOs stay locked in tune; DCOs drift unpredictably
VCOs are software plugins; DCOs are hardware
VCOs are monophonic; DCOs are always polyphonic

questions.expert_explanation: Analogue VCOs drift slightly in pitch as components warm up, giving vintage warmth, whereas DCOs use a digital clock to stay rock-solid in tune.

expert_quote.text: A DCO gives you authentic analogue warmth without having to stop the show to re-tune your synthesiser.
expert_quote.author: Roland Engineering Archives

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Analogue VCOs drift slightly in pitch as components warm up, giving vintage warmth, whereas DCOs use a digital clock to stay rock-solid in tune.

explanation_image.alt: Q17: VCO vs DCO Tuning Difference

questions.title: Q18: Principles of FM Synthesis
questions.content: How does FM (Frequency Modulation) synthesis, like on the Yamaha DX7, create sound?

answers.text: Filters white noise through a resonant LPF
One oscillator modulates another at audio rates

questions.expert_explanation: FM synthesis uses a modulator oscillator to vary a carrier oscillator's pitch at audio speeds, creating bright metallic sidebands ideal for bells and electric pianos.

expert_quote.text: FM synthesis unlocked shimmering metallic bells and punchy digital keys that analogue subtractive filters could never produce.
expert_quote.author: Digital Sound Synthesis Pioneers

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: FM synthesis uses a modulator oscillator to vary a carrier oscillator's pitch at audio speeds, creating bright metallic sidebands ideal for bells and electric pianos.

questions.title: Q19: Wavetable Synthesis Scanning & Morphing
questions.content: How does wavetable synthesis create evolving, shifting sounds?

answers.text: Detunes two analogue oscillators for pitch drift
Scans smoothly through a bank of single-cycle waves
Sweeps a resonant filter over a static sawtooth
Triggers random slices of a recorded drum loop

questions.expert_explanation: A wavetable oscillator morphs smoothly across a table of different single-cycle digital waveforms, creating rich, animated timbres when modulated by an LFO or envelope.

expert_quote.text: Wavetable synthesis took us beyond static analogue shapes—by scanning through a table of waveforms, timbre becomes a living, moving landscape.
expert_quote.author: Wolfgang Palm (PPG Wave Creator)

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: A wavetable oscillator morphs smoothly across a table of different single-cycle digital waveforms, creating rich, animated timbres when modulated by an LFO or envelope.

questions.title: Q20: Filter Self-Oscillation at Maximum Resonance
questions.content: What happens when an analogue filter enters self-oscillation at maximum resonance?

answers.text: It switches into high-pass mode automatically
It mutes all output to protect the circuit
It locks the oscillators to a digital clock
It generates its own pure sine-wave pitch

questions.expert_explanation: At maximum resonance, positive feedback makes the filter ring continuously as a pure sine wave tuned to the cutoff frequency — even with no oscillator feeding it.

expert_quote.text: Crank the resonance to ten and you no longer need an oscillator—the filter becomes its own instrument, singing pure sine waves.
expert_quote.author: Bob Moog

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: At maximum resonance, positive feedback makes the filter ring continuously as a pure sine wave tuned to the cutoff frequency — even with no oscillator feeding it.

explanation_image.alt: Q20: Filter Self-Oscillation at Maximum Resonance

items.title: Topic 4: Sampling (Part 1)
items.description: Mastery quiz covering the fundamentals of Sampling.

questions.title: Q1: What is Audio Sampling?
questions.content: What is audio sampling in music production?

answers.text: Boosting bass with a graphic equaliser
Recording real sound to play back on a sampler
Converting MIDI notes into sheet music

questions.expert_explanation: Audio sampling captures a snippet of real recorded sound (like a drum hit or vocal) so a sampler can trigger, pitch, loop, or rearrange it via MIDI.

expert_quote.text: Sampling transformed recorded sound into a playable musical instrument, forever reshaping hip-hop, dance music, and contemporary composition.
expert_quote.author: Edexcel Music Technology Specification

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Audio sampling captures a snippet of real recorded sound (like a drum hit or vocal) so a sampler can trigger, pitch, loop, or rearrange it via MIDI.

questions.title: Q2: Sample Truncation
questions.content: What does truncating an audio sample mean?

answers.text: Trimming unwanted silence from the start or end
Stretching a sample to double its length
Reversing the audio so it plays backwards
Adding heavy stereo reverb to the tail

questions.expert_explanation: Truncation removes dead silence before the attack transient and after the decay tail, ensuring instant MIDI triggering and saving sampler memory.

expert_quote.text: Tight truncation is essential for punchy beats—if there is even 10 milliseconds of silence before your drum transient, your sequence will feel sluggish and off-beat.
expert_quote.author: Hip-Hop Production Techniques

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Truncation removes dead silence before the attack transient and after the decay tail, ensuring instant MIDI triggering and saving sampler memory.

questions.title: Q3: Crossfade Looping
questions.content: Why is a crossfade applied to the loop points of a sustained sample?

answers.text: To transpose the sample up one octave
To convert a stereo sample into mono
To increase the sample rate to 96 kHz
To blend loop edges smoothly without clicks

questions.expert_explanation: Crossfade looping overlaps and fades the end of a loop into its start so sustained notes (like strings or pads) cycle seamlessly with zero clicks or pops.

expert_quote.text: Without a crossfade, looping an organic acoustic instrument is nearly impossible—the tiniest phase clash will sound like a broken needle ticking on vinyl.
expert_quote.author: Sound Design Principles

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Crossfade looping overlaps and fades the end of a loop into its start so sustained notes (like strings or pads) cycle seamlessly with zero clicks or pops.

questions.title: Q4: Practical Task — Sample Preparation Order
questions.content: Order the steps for preparing a raw drum sample from START (top) to FINISH (bottom).
questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Always import the raw recording first, truncate dead air before the hit, cut at zero-crossings to prevent clicks, and finally map the sample to keys with an ADSR envelope.

expert_quote.text: A sampler is only as tight as your front truncation. Even a 5ms delay before the kick transient will destroy the groove of your rhythm section.
expert_quote.author: Roger Linn, Inventor of the LM-1 & Akai MPC

questions.expert_explanation: Always import the raw recording first, truncate dead air before the hit, cut at zero-crossings to prevent clicks, and finally map the sample to keys with an ADSR envelope.

explanation_image.alt: Q4: Practical Task — Sample Preparation Order

questions.title: Q5: Reversing a Sample
questions.content: What happens to a sound's envelope when an audio sample is reversed?

answers.text: It shifts down by one full musical octave
It swells backwards into a sharp cutoff
It removes all frequencies below 500 Hz
It quantises every transient to 1/16th notes

questions.expert_explanation: Reversing a percussive sound (like a cymbal or snare) flips its fast attack and long decay into a slow, rising suction swell that ends abruptly — ideal for transitions.

expert_quote.text: A reversed crash cymbal or vocal reverb tail is the quintessential tension-builder—it pulls the listener forward right into the downbeat.
expert_quote.author: Mixing & Production Standards

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Reversing a percussive sound (like a cymbal or snare) flips its fast attack and long decay into a slow, rising suction swell that ends abruptly — ideal for transitions.

questions.title: Q6: Stretching One Sample Across a Keyboard
questions.content: What happens if you map one single vocal or instrument sample across an entire keyboard?

answers.text: It stays natural and realistic on every key
It automatically harmonises into major chords
Extreme notes sound unnatural ('chipmunk' or slow)
It disables the sampler's low-pass filter

questions.expert_explanation: Pushing a single sample far from its root pitch shifts its formants and speed, causing high notes to sound chipmunk-like and low notes to sound sluggish and muddy.

expert_quote.text: You can span a synth sound or a 909 kick across a few keys, but spanning an acoustic piano across three octaves instantly ruins the illusion of reality.
expert_quote.author: Sampler Programming Manual

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Pushing a single sample far from its root pitch shifts its formants and speed, causing high notes to sound chipmunk-like and low notes to sound sluggish and muddy.

explanation_image.alt: Q6: Stretching One Sample Across a Keyboard

questions.title: Q7: Stutter Editing
questions.content: What is a 'stutter edit' in modern audio editing?

answers.text: Rapidly repeating a tiny audio slice on the grid
Fading a vocal out slowly over four bars
Layering three acoustic guitars in stereo
Applying gentle high-pass filtering at 80 Hz

questions.expert_explanation: A stutter edit copies and rapidly repeats a short rhythmic slice (such as a 1/16th or 1/32nd vocal syllable) to build tension before a chorus or EDM drop.

expert_quote.text: The stutter edit turns vocal syllables and drum hits into rhythmic percussion instruments, breaking repetitive loops with explosive electronic energy.
expert_quote.author: Electronic Music Production Guide

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: A stutter edit copies and rapidly repeats a short rhythmic slice (such as a 1/16th or 1/32nd vocal syllable) to build tension before a chorus or EDM drop.

questions.title: Q8: Classic Sampler Pitching (Varispeed)
questions.content: In traditional sampler playback without time-stretching, what happens when you pitch a sample up?

answers.text: It plays slower and lasts much longer
Its length and speed stay completely unchanged
Its stereo width collapses straight to mono
It plays faster and finishes sooner

questions.expert_explanation: Without digital time-stretching, pitching a sample up speeds up playback (just like speeding up tape or vinyl), making the sample shorter and brighter.

expert_quote.text: On classic samplers like the SP-1200 or Akai MPC, tuning up a sample always makes it play faster—it is the foundational physics of tape and digital sample replay.
expert_quote.author: Vintage Sampler Architecture

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Without digital time-stretching, pitching a sample up speeds up playback (just like speeding up tape or vinyl), making the sample shorter and brighter.

questions.title: Q9: Why Use Multi-Sampling?
questions.content: Why do realistic sample libraries (like acoustic pianos) use multi-sampling?

answers.text: To reduce the hard-drive file size to under 1 MB
To keep tone natural across all pitches and dynamics
To force every note to play at the same volume
To replace all acoustic recordings with sine waves

questions.expert_explanation: Multi-sampling records separate samples across different key zones and velocity layers, avoiding artificial pitch-stretching artefacts and capturing realistic dynamic tone.

expert_quote.text: Multisampling is what separates a cheap toy keyboard synth from a multi-gigabyte concert grand piano library that fools even trained classical ears.
expert_quote.author: Virtual Instrument Design

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Multi-sampling records separate samples across different key zones and velocity layers, avoiding artificial pitch-stretching artefacts and capturing realistic dynamic tone.

questions.title: Q10: Creative Low-Pass Filtering on Samples
questions.content: How is a low-pass filter (LPF) used creatively on audio samples?

answers.text: To boost harsh cymbals above 12 kHz
To pitch-shift vocals up by a fifth
To sweep brightness down for lo-fi or build-ups
To add stereo delay echoes to snare hits

questions.expert_explanation: Rolling off highs with an LPF warms up bright samples for lo-fi hip hop, while automating the cutoff upward creates classic filter-sweep build-ups in dance music.

expert_quote.text: Sweeping a low-pass filter over a sampled disco loop is one of the most powerful tension-and-release tricks in modern dance music.
expert_quote.author: House Music Production Manual

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Rolling off highs with an LPF warms up bright samples for lo-fi hip hop, while automating the cutoff upward creates classic filter-sweep build-ups in dance music.

explanation_image.alt: Q10: Creative Low-Pass Filtering on Samples

items.title: Topic 4: Sampling (Part 2)
items.description: Mastery quiz covering the fundamentals of Sampling.

questions.title: Q11: Sampler Root Note Transposition
questions.content: A piano sample has its root note set to C4. What happens when you trigger note E4?

answers.text: It plays down 4 semitones and sounds slower
It pitches up 4 semitones (a major third)
It stays locked at C4 regardless of the key
It switches automatically to a square wave

questions.expert_explanation: When a sample's root note is C4, playing E4 transposes it up 4 semitones (a major third) so the sampler tracks the keyboard melodically.

expert_quote.text: Setting accurate root notes is the first rule of multisampling—if the root note is wrongly mapped, every key you play will be out of tune.
expert_quote.author: Virtual Instrument Programming

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: When a sample's root note is C4, playing E4 transposes it up 4 semitones (a major third) so the sampler tracks the keyboard melodically.

questions.title: Q12: Round Robin Drum Sampling
questions.content: What is the primary purpose of 'round robin' sampling in drum plugins?

answers.text: To pan every snare hit automatically left to right
To loop a short cymbal hit indefinitely
To layer a sine sub-bass under every tom
To cycle alternate hits and avoid 'machine-gun' repetition

questions.expert_explanation: Round robin cycles through several slightly different recordings of the same drum hit so fast snare rolls sound natural instead of robotic and 'machine-gun'-like.

expert_quote.text: Round robin restores human imperfection to sampled performances by ensuring no two consecutive notes share the exact same micro-transients.
expert_quote.author: Sample Library Design

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Round robin cycles through several slightly different recordings of the same drum hit so fast snare rolls sound natural instead of robotic and 'machine-gun'-like.

questions.title: Q13: Time-Stretching Artefacts
questions.content: What causes phasey or metallic artefacts when extreme time-stretching is applied to audio?

answers.text: Repeating and overlapping tiny audio grains/slices
Running a 24-bit file through an analogue console
Recording with phantom power switched on
Using a low-pass filter below 10 kHz

questions.expert_explanation: Extreme time-stretching duplicates and crossfades tiny slices of audio to fill extra time, which introduces audible metallic phasing and smeared transients.

expert_quote.text: Time stretching decouples tempo from pitch, but extreme stretching pushes phase-alignment mathematics to its limits, smearing transient crispness.
expert_quote.author: DSP Audio Algorithms

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Extreme time-stretching duplicates and crossfades tiny slices of audio to fill extra time, which introduces audible metallic phasing and smeared transients.

questions.title: Q14: Bit Crushing & Quantisation Noise
questions.content: What does a bit crusher plugin do to change the sound of a sample?

answers.text: Raises bit depth to 32-bit for cleaner headroom
Reduces bit depth, adding gritty quantisation noise

questions.expert_explanation: A bit crusher lowers the bit depth (e.g., from 16-bit down to 8-bit or 4-bit), increasing quantisation error for a crunchy, lo-fi digital grit.

expert_quote.text: Bit crushing lowers the dynamic resolution, trading pristine digital transparency for explosive lo-fi crunch and aggressive punch.
expert_quote.author: Sound Design & Synthesis Guide

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: A bit crusher lowers the bit depth (e.g., from 16-bit down to 8-bit or 4-bit), increasing quantisation error for a crunchy, lo-fi digital grit.

questions.title: Q15: Aliasing & Downsampling
questions.content: What causes audible 'aliasing' when reducing the sample rate of digital audio?

answers.text: Adding too much analogue plate reverb
Frequencies above half the sample rate folding back
Recording quieter than -24 dBFS on a preamp
Panning two stereo tracks hard left and right

questions.expert_explanation: By the Nyquist theorem, any frequency above half the sample rate cannot be captured accurately and folds back into the audible spectrum as harsh, metallic aliasing.

expert_quote.text: Aliasing is digital audio's mirror trick—ultrasonic frequencies that exceed the Nyquist wall reflect back as discordant metallic ghosts.
expert_quote.author: Principles of Digital Audio

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: By the Nyquist theorem, any frequency above half the sample rate cannot be captured accurately and folds back into the audible spectrum as harsh, metallic aliasing.

questions.title: Q16: MIDI Middle C Note Number
questions.content: In the standard MIDI specification, what note number represents Middle C (C4)?
questions.expert_explanation: In standard MIDI note numbering (0–127), Note 60 is Middle C. Each semitone step adds or subtracts 1, so one octave up is 72 and one octave down is 48.

expert_quote.text: Note 60 is the universal anchor point of the MIDI specification—the central pivot around which all keyboard mapping rotates.
expert_quote.author: MIDI Association Standard

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: In standard MIDI note numbering (0–127), Note 60 is Middle C. Each semitone step adds or subtracts 1, so one octave up is 72 and one octave down is 48.

explanation_image.alt: Q16: MIDI Middle C Note Number

questions.title: Q17: 7-Bit MIDI Velocity Range
questions.content: In the standard 7-bit MIDI protocol, what is the valid numerical range for note velocity?
questions.expert_explanation: MIDI velocity is encoded as a 7-bit data byte, giving 128 steps from 0 to 127 (with 1–127 for sounding notes and 0 acting as Note Off).

expert_quote.text: A 7-bit architecture gave MIDI 128 velocity levels—more than enough nuance to capture subtle expressive touch from keyboard players in 1983.
expert_quote.author: History of Music Technology

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: MIDI velocity is encoded as a 7-bit data byte, giving 128 steps from 0 to 127 (with 1–127 for sounding notes and 0 acting as Note Off).

questions.title: Q18: Fixing Stuck MIDI Notes
questions.content: If a synthesiser note keeps ringing endlessly after you release the key, how do you stop it?

answers.text: Turn up the master stereo reverb send
Double the project tempo in the DAW
Send a MIDI 'All Notes Off' (Panic) message

questions.expert_explanation: A stuck note happens when a MIDI Note Off message is missed. Sending an 'All Notes Off' (MIDI CC123 / Panic) command silences every active voice immediately.

expert_quote.text: Every live keyboardist has needed the MIDI Panic button at least once—it is the digital reset switch that forces stuck envelopes to close.
expert_quote.author: Live Keyboard Rig Guide

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: A stuck note happens when a MIDI Note Off message is missed. Sending an 'All Notes Off' (MIDI CC123 / Panic) command silences every active voice immediately.

questions.title: Q19: MIDI System Exclusive (SysEx)
questions.content: Why are MIDI System Exclusive (SysEx) files used in music production?

answers.text: To back up or load synth patches and firmware
To quantise live acoustic drum recordings
To apply stereo widening across a master bus

questions.expert_explanation: MIDI System Exclusive (SysEx) carries manufacturer-specific data, letting musicians back up custom synthesiser patch banks or update hardware firmware over MIDI.

expert_quote.text: Standard MIDI tells the musician how to play the song; SysEx tells the machine how to build the instrument.
expert_quote.author: Synthesizer Systems Architecture

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: MIDI System Exclusive (SysEx) carries manufacturer-specific data, letting musicians back up custom synthesiser patch banks or update hardware firmware over MIDI.

questions.title: Q20: MIDI Data vs Audio Playback
questions.content: Why can the exact same standard MIDI file sound completely different on two different computers?

answers.text: MIDI files compress audio heavily like MP3s
MIDI files change tempo randomly on export
MIDI cables only carry mono low frequencies
MIDI holds note data, not audio — each synth sounds different

questions.expert_explanation: A MIDI file contains performance instructions (notes, timing, velocity) rather than recorded audio, so its sound depends entirely on whichever virtual instrument or synth plays it back.

expert_quote.text: MIDI is digital sheet music, not recorded sound. The performance is only as good as the sound engine that reads the notes.
expert_quote.author: Edexcel Music Technology Specification

questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: A MIDI file contains performance instructions (notes, timing, velocity) rather than recorded audio, so its sound depends entirely on whichever virtual instrument or synth plays it back.

items.title: Topic 5: Dynamic Processing (Part 1)
items.description: Mastery quiz covering the fundamentals of Dynamic Processing.

questions.title: Q1: Dynamic Range
questions.content: What does 'dynamic range' mean in audio recording?

answers.text: Quietest and loudest levels of an audio signal
Level difference between left and right channels
Headroom gap between tape saturation and clipping

questions.expert_explanation: Dynamic range is the decibel difference between the quietest audible sound (or system noise floor) and the loudest unclipped peak.

expert_quote.text: Dynamic range is musical breathing room; squashing it entirely robs music of life.
expert_quote.author: Bob Katz

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: Dynamic range is the decibel difference between the quietest audible sound (or system noise floor) and the loudest unclipped peak.

"Dynamic range is musical breathing room; squashing it entirely robs music of life."
- Bob Katz

questions.title: Practical Listening: Dynamics A/B Comparison
questions.content: Listen to Audio A (Dry) and Audio B (Wet). What dynamic processing has been applied to Audio B?
options: Fast noise gating to mute spill
questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Audio B clamps down pick attack transients while raising sustaining harmonics. This compresses dynamic range and significantly increases perceived guitar sustain.

expert_quote.text: Compression isn't just volume control; it's an envelope shaper. It glues the performance together and locks the instrument into the pocket.
expert_quote.author: Chris Lord-Alge, Mix Engineer (Green Day, Muse)

questions.expert_explanation: Audio B clamps down pick attack transients while raising sustaining harmonics. This compresses dynamic range and significantly increases perceived guitar sustain.

questions.title: Practical Task: Compressor Internal Signal Routing
questions.content: Place the internal stages of an audio compressor into the correct processing order (input to output).
questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: The input signal enters the buffer and feeds both the detector circuit and the VCA. The detector calculates necessary attenuation against threshold, driving the VCA before make-up gain restores overall level.

expert_quote.text: Understanding the detector circuit is the key to mastering sidechain compression, vocal ducking, and de-essing.
expert_quote.author: Rupert Neve, Audio Electronics Designer

questions.expert_explanation: The input signal enters the buffer and feeds both the detector circuit and the VCA. The detector calculates necessary attenuation against threshold, driving the VCA before make-up gain restores overall level.

questions.title: Q4: Compressor Attack Time
questions.content: What does the attack time control on a compressor?

answers.text: Speed of gain reduction above threshold
Decibel level needed to trigger compression

questions.expert_explanation: Attack time dictates how quickly the compressor attenuates the signal once it exceeds threshold. Fast attack catches transients, while slow attack lets initial punch pass through.

expert_quote.text: Attack time shapes the punch of drums: too fast and you kill the snap, too slow and peaks escape.
expert_quote.author: Al Schmitt

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: Attack time dictates how quickly the compressor attenuates the signal once it exceeds threshold. Fast attack catches transients, while slow attack lets initial punch pass through.

"Attack time shapes the punch of drums: too fast and you kill the snap, too slow and peaks escape."
- Al Schmitt

questions.title: Q5: Compressor Release Time
questions.content: What does the release time control on a compressor?

answers.text: Speed of returning to normal level below threshold
Amount of ratio applied to peaks above threshold
Decibel level where gain reduction begins to trigger
Speed of clamping initial transients across threshold

questions.expert_explanation: Release time controls how quickly the compressor stops attenuating and returns to unity gain once the signal drops back below threshold.

expert_quote.text: Release time must groove with the tempo of the music to prevent unnatural pumping.
expert_quote.author: Tony Maserati

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: Release time controls how quickly the compressor stops attenuating and returns to unity gain once the signal drops back below threshold.

"Release time must groove with the tempo of the music to prevent unnatural pumping."
- Tony Maserati

questions.title: Q6: Hard Knee vs Soft Knee
questions.content: How does a soft-knee compressor differ from a hard-knee compressor?

answers.text: It applies compression abruptly when threshold is crossed
It boosts quiet passages rather than attenuating loud peaks
It applies a steep low-pass filter to tame harsh vocal sibilance
It applies gain reduction gradually as signal approaches threshold

questions.expert_explanation: A hard knee applies the full ratio abruptly when the threshold is crossed. A soft knee introduces compression gradually over a transition curve for smoother control.

expert_quote.text: Soft knee curves provide transparent, musical compression on vocals and acoustic instruments.
expert_quote.author: Paul White

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: A hard knee applies the full ratio abruptly when the threshold is crossed. A soft knee introduces compression gradually over a transition curve for smoother control.

"Soft knee curves provide transparent, musical compression on vocals and acoustic instruments."
- Paul White

questions.title: Q7: Extreme Compression Ratios
questions.content: A compressor set with an extreme ratio of infinity-to-one (∞:1) acts as what device?
questions.expert_explanation: An ∞:1 ratio prevents the audio signal from exceeding the ceiling under any circumstance, turning the compressor into a brickwall peak limiter.

expert_quote.text: A limiter is simply an aggressive compressor with a very high ratio and instantaneous attack.
expert_quote.author: Bob Ludwig

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: An ∞:1 ratio prevents the audio signal from exceeding the ceiling under any circumstance, turning the compressor into a brickwall peak limiter.

"A limiter is simply an aggressive compressor with a very high ratio and instantaneous attack."
- Bob Ludwig

questions.title: Q8: Make-Up Gain
questions.content: Why does audio sound louder after compression and make-up gain, even if peak levels are unchanged?

answers.text: Panning is widened to double perceived volume
Phase cancellation focuses energy in the midrange
Peaks are lowered so average RMS level can be raised
Analogue harmonics double physical acoustic pressure

questions.expert_explanation: Compression lowers the loudest peaks to reduce dynamic range. Make-up gain can then boost the entire signal, raising the average RMS energy without clipping.

expert_quote.text: Compression reduces peak-to-average ratio; make-up gain is what actually makes the track sound louder.
expert_quote.author: Dave Pensado

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: Compression lowers the loudest peaks to reduce dynamic range. Make-up gain can then boost the entire signal, raising the average RMS energy without clipping.

"Compression reduces peak-to-average ratio; make-up gain is what actually makes the track sound louder."
- Dave Pensado

questions.title: Q9: Gain Reduction Calculation
questions.content: A compressor has a threshold of -6 dB and a ratio of 2:1. If an audio peak hits 0 dB, what is the gain reduction?
questions.expert_explanation: The peak exceeds the -6 dB threshold by 6 dB (0 dB - (-6 dB) = 6 dB). With a 2:1 ratio, the overshoot is halved to 3 dB, resulting in 3 dB of gain reduction.

expert_quote.text: Understanding the gain reduction math proves exactly what the meters are showing you.
expert_quote.author: Roey Izhaki

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: The peak exceeds the -6 dB threshold by 6 dB (0 dB - (-6 dB) = 6 dB). With a 2:1 ratio, the overshoot is halved to 3 dB, resulting in 3 dB of gain reduction.

"Understanding the gain reduction math proves exactly what the metres are showing you."
- Roey Izhaki

questions.title: Q10: Troubleshooting Gain Reduction
questions.content: If a compressor's gain reduction meter stays stuck showing heavy reduction even when no audio plays, what is the cause?

answers.text: Threshold is too low or release is too slow
Ratio is too low to create noticeable reduction
Attack time is too fast to catch drum transients
Make-up gain is set too high, clipping output

questions.expert_explanation: If the meter stays pinned at heavy reduction, either the threshold is set below the background noise floor, or release is set too long to recover between audio passages.

expert_quote.text: If the needle never moves, you are not compressing dynamic transients—you are just turning the fader down with extra distortion.
expert_quote.author: Chris Lord-Alge

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: If the meter stays pinned at heavy reduction, either the threshold is set below the background noise floor, or release is set too long to recover between audio passages.

"If the needle never moves, you are not compressing dynamic transients—you are just turning the fader down with extra distortion."
- Chris Lord-Alge

items.title: Topic 5: Dynamic Processing (Part 2)
items.description: Mastery quiz covering the fundamentals of Dynamic Processing.

questions.title: Q11: Noise Gate Operating Principle & Threshold
questions.content: What is the primary purpose of a noise gate in audio production?

answers.text: Boost quiet passages to match loud peaks
Compress loud peaks to prevent clipping
Mute audio falling below a threshold level
Filter out treble hiss from microphones

questions.expert_explanation: A noise gate mutes or attenuates any audio dropping below a set threshold, removing unwanted mic bleed and background hum.

expert_quote.text: Gates clean up tom bleed and amp hiss, but set the threshold carefully to avoid chattering.
expert_quote.author: Hugh Robjohns

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: A noise gate mutes or attenuates any audio dropping below a set threshold, removing unwanted mic bleed and background hum.

"Gates clean up tom bleed and amp hiss, but set the threshold carefully to avoid chattering."
- Hugh Robjohns

questions.title: Q12: Practical Task — Setting a Noise Gate Threshold
questions.content: Move the gate threshold fader to mute the hi-hat bleed without cutting off the snare hits.
questions.label: Gate Threshold
questions.expert_explanation: Setting the threshold around -18 dB sits safely above the -32 dB hi-hat bleed while allowing every -6 dB snare hit to open the gate cleanly.
questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Setting the threshold around -18 dB sits safely above the -32 dB hi-hat bleed while allowing every -6 dB snare hit to open the gate cleanly.

questions.title: Q13: Noise Gate Envelope (Attack, Hold, and Release)
questions.content: What does the 'hold' control do on a noise gate?

answers.text: Delays opening the gate when peaks cross threshold
Keeps the gate open before release begins
Locks the threshold level during playback
Sets maximum attenuation when the gate shuts

questions.expert_explanation: Hold sets how long the gate stays 100% open after the signal drops below threshold before the release phase begins.

expert_quote.text: Hold time is essential on toms: it lets the drum ring breathe naturally before the gate snaps closed.
expert_quote.author: Mike Senior

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: Hold sets how long the gate stays 100% open after the signal drops below threshold before the release phase begins.

"Hold time is essential on toms: it lets the drum ring breathe naturally before the gate snaps closed."
- Mike Senior

questions.title: Practical Task: Gate Hold Time for Tom Sustain
questions.content: Move the gate hold fader so the floor tom body sustains cleanly before the gate begins closing.
questions.label: Gate Hold Time
questions.expert_explanation: Setting hold around 150–250 ms keeps the gate 100% open while the low-frequency tom shell rings out, preventing an unnatural early cut-off.
questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Setting hold around 150–250 ms keeps the gate 100% open while the low-frequency tom shell rings out, preventing an unnatural early cut-off.

questions.title: Q14: Gating Drum Spill on Snare and Kick Mics
questions.content: Why do audio engineers use noise gates on close-miked snare and tom tracks?

answers.text: To compress drum transients and boost shell ring
To add stereo reverb width across the kit
To align phase between top and bottom mics
To silence cymbal bleed and spill between hits

questions.expert_explanation: Close drum mics pick up loud cymbal spill and bleed from other drums. Gating silences the mic between hits to keep the kit punchy and clean.

expert_quote.text: Gating drum bleed gives you discrete punch and stops hi-hat spill from washing out your snare processing.
expert_quote.author: Chris Lord-Alge

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: Close drum mics pick up loud cymbal spill and bleed from other drums. Gating silences the mic between hits to keep the kit punchy and clean.

"Gating drum bleed gives you discrete punch and stops hi-hat spill from washing out your snare processing."
- Chris Lord-Alge

questions.title: Q15: Gate Sidechain / Key Input Triggering
questions.content: How does an external sidechain (key input) control a noise gate?

answers.text: Links gate threshold to project tempo
Uses an external signal to trigger the gate
Duplicates gate output to a stereo delay
Fixes phase cancellation between stereo tracks

questions.expert_explanation: Sidechain keying allows a separate audio track (like a kick drum) to trigger the gate open on another track (like a sub-bass).

expert_quote.text: Keying a noise gate from a kick drum to trigger a sub-bass sine tone is the classic trick for earth-shaking low end.
expert_quote.author: Dave Pensado

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: Sidechain keying allows a separate audio track (like a kick drum) to trigger the gate open on another track (like a sub-bass).

"Keying a noise gate from a kick drum to trigger a sub-bass sine tone is the classic trick for earth-shaking low end."
- Dave Pensado

questions.title: Practical Task: Gate Release Time for Guitar Decay
questions.content: Move the gate release fader so the decaying guitar chord fades out naturally without chopping off early.
questions.label: Gate Release Time
questions.expert_explanation: A slower release time (around 600–900 ms) lets the gate close gradually along the natural decay of the guitar chord instead of chopping off the tail abruptly.
questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: A slower release time (around 600–900 ms) lets the gate close gradually along the natural decay of the guitar chord instead of chopping off the tail abruptly.

questions.title: Q16: Gate Hysteresis & Dual Threshold Mechanics
questions.content: What does the 'hysteresis' setting do on an advanced noise gate?

answers.text: Links left and right detectors for stereo width
Speeds up attack times on fast transients
Sets separate thresholds to open and close
Adds vintage tape saturation to gated audio

questions.expert_explanation: Hysteresis uses a higher threshold to open the gate and a lower threshold to close it, preventing chattering on decaying notes.

expert_quote.text: Hysteresis prevents gate chattering by making sure the signal has to drop significantly lower before the gate shuts.
expert_quote.author: Paul White

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: Hysteresis uses a higher threshold to open the gate and a lower threshold to close it, preventing chattering on decaying notes.

"Hysteresis prevents gate chattering by making sure the signal has to drop significantly lower before the gate shuts."
- Paul White

questions.title: Q17: The 1980s Gated Snare Reverb Technique
questions.content: How was the famous 1980s gated snare drum sound created?

answers.text: Reverse tape echo with a sweeping filter
A loud snare reverb tail cut off by a gate
A flanger blended with drum overheads
Heavy tube distortion on console channels

questions.expert_explanation: Pioneered by Hugh Padgham and Phil Collins, gated reverb uses a noise gate to abruptly chop off a massive snare reverb tail.

expert_quote.text: The SSL listen mic compressor slammed the room reverb, and the gate slammed it shut—defining the drum sound of the 1980s.
expert_quote.author: Hugh Padgham

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: Pioneered by Hugh Padgham and Phil Collins, gated reverb uses a noise gate to abruptly chop off a massive snare reverb tail.

"The SSL listen mic compressor slammed the room reverb, and the gate slammed it shut—defining the drum sound of the 1980s."
- Hugh Padgham

questions.title: Practical Task: Smooth Gate Attack Time for Strings
questions.content: Set a slower gate attack time so a bowed string pad fades in smoothly without clicking or sounding abrupt.
questions.label: Gate Attack Time
questions.expert_explanation: Setting a 0 ms attack causes an audible click, while a slower attack (15–35 ms) lets the gate open smoothly for gentle instruments like bowed strings or pads.
questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Setting a 0 ms attack causes an audible click, while a slower attack (15–35 ms) lets the gate open smoothly for gentle instruments like bowed strings or pads.

questions.title: Q18: Practical Task — Noise Gate Attack Time
questions.content: Set a fast gate attack time (1–5 ms) to preserve the snare transient without causing a 0 ms click.
questions.label: Gate Attack Time
questions.expert_explanation: Setting 0 ms causes an instantaneous amplitude jump and an audible click, whereas 1–5 ms opens fast enough to keep the snare transient intact cleanly.
questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Setting 0 ms causes an instantaneous amplitude jump and an audible click, whereas 1–5 ms opens fast enough to keep the snare transient intact cleanly.

questions.title: Q19: Noise Gate Floor / Range Control
questions.content: What does the 'range' or 'floor' control do on a noise gate?

answers.text: Controls make-up gain added to the output
Sets frequency band analysed by detector
Controls how fast gain reduction resets
Sets maximum attenuation when gate closes

questions.expert_explanation: Range (or floor) limits how many decibels the gate attenuates when closed, allowing natural room bleed (-15 dB) instead of total silence.

expert_quote.text: Never mute bleed completely if you don't have to; setting a 12 dB floor keeps the kit sounding cohesive and natural.
expert_quote.author: Roey Izhaki

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: Range (or floor) limits how many decibels the gate attenuates when closed, allowing natural room bleed (-15 dB) instead of total silence.

"Never mute bleed completely if you don't have to; setting a 12 dB floor keeps the kit sounding cohesive and natural."
- Roey Izhaki

questions.title: Q20: Troubleshooting Gate Chattering & False Retriggering
questions.content: Why does a noise gate sometimes rapidly 'chatter' (open and close repeatedly) on a decaying drum hit?

answers.text: Audio level fluctuates right on the threshold
Microphone polarity is inverted in mono
Gate range is set to complete silence
Gate attack time is set too slow

questions.expert_explanation: Chattering happens when a decaying signal hovers right around the threshold, rapidly triggering the gate open and shut.

expert_quote.text: If a gate chatters, either lengthen your hold time so the decay rings out, or widen the hysteresis window.
expert_quote.author: Mike Senior

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: Chattering happens when a decaying signal hovers right around the threshold, rapidly triggering the gate open and shut.

"If a gate chatters, either lengthen your hold time so the decay rings out, or widen the hysteresis window."
- Mike Senior

items.title: Topic 6: EQ & Stereo (Part 1)
items.description: Mastery quiz covering the fundamentals of EQ & Stereo.

questions.title: Q1: Equalisation (EQ) Definition & Frequency Spectrum Balance
questions.content: In music production, what is the main purpose of an equaliser (EQ)?

answers.text: Control dynamic range between loud and quiet
Add artificial room reverb and stereo depth
Correct out-of-tune pitch errors on vocals

questions.expert_explanation: Equalisation (EQ) adjusts the relative volume of specific frequency bands to shape tone, clarity, and mix separation.

expert_quote.text: EQ is about balance. You can't boost something that isn't there, but you can carve away the clutter to let what is there shine.
expert_quote.author: George Massenburg

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: Equalisation (EQ) adjusts the relative volume of specific frequency bands to shape tone, clarity, and mix separation.

"EQ is about balance. You can't boost something that isn't there, but you can carve away the clutter to let what is there shine."
- George Massenburg

questions.title: Q2: Equalisation Fundamentals: Cut and Boost Gain Controls
questions.content: In audio equalisation, what is the difference between a 'cut' and a 'boost'?

answers.text: Boost widens stereo; cut narrows to mono
Boost widens bandwidth; cut narrows curve
Boost raises volume; cut lowers volume
Boost limits peaks; cut mutes quiet noise

questions.expert_explanation: A boost increases the decibel level of a frequency band, whereas a cut reduces its level—often preferred to remove muddiness cleanly.

expert_quote.text: Subtractive EQ is the secret to clarity. Carve away what you don't need before you even think about boosting.
expert_quote.author: Sylvia Massy

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: A boost increases the decibel level of a frequency band, whereas a cut reduces its level—often preferred to remove muddiness cleanly.

"Subtractive EQ is the secret to clarity. Carve away what you don't need before you even think about boosting."
- Sylvia Massy

questions.title: Q3: Parametric EQ Controls: What is the Q Factor?
questions.content: On a parametric EQ, what does the 'Q' (Quality Factor) control?

answers.text: Overall master volume of the track
Width or sharpness of the bell curve
Stereo pan position left to right
Attack and release speed of the circuit

questions.expert_explanation: The Q (Quality Factor) controls the bandwidth of a parametric EQ bell curve: low Q is wide and musical, while high Q is narrow and surgical.

expert_quote.text: Boost wide for tone, cut narrow for problems. The Q knob is your control over how surgical you want to be.
expert_quote.author: Mixing Proverb

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: The Q (Quality Factor) controls the bandwidth of a parametric EQ bell curve: low Q is wide and musical, while high Q is narrow and surgical.

"Boost wide for tone, cut narrow for problems. The Q knob is your control over how surgical you want to be."
- Mixing Proverb

questions.title: Q4: High-Pass Filter (Low-Cut) for Vocal Clarity
questions.content: Which filter should you use to remove low-frequency plosives and mic stand rumble from a vocal?
questions.expert_explanation: A High-Pass Filter (HPF) removes low frequencies below the cutoff (e.g. 80–120 Hz) to eliminate mic stand rumble and vocal plosives.

expert_quote.text: High-pass filtering everything except the kick drum and bass guitar is the quickest way to create headroom and eliminate low-end mud in a mix.
expert_quote.author: Bobby Owsinski

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: A High-Pass Filter (HPF) removes low frequencies below the cutoff (e.g. 80–120 Hz) to eliminate mic stand rumble and vocal plosives.

"High-pass filtering everything except the kick drum and bass guitar is the quickest way to create headroom and eliminate low-end mud in a mix."
- Bobby Owsinski

questions.title: Q5: High-Shelf Filter Operating Principles
questions.content: What frequencies does a high-shelf filter adjust?

answers.text: All frequencies below the selected corner frequency
Only one narrow notch at the centre frequency
All frequencies above the selected corner frequency
Frequencies restricted strictly to the sub-bass register

questions.expert_explanation: A high-shelf filter boosts or cuts all frequencies uniformly above its corner frequency, ideal for adding air or taming harshness.

expert_quote.text: Shelving EQs are great for adding broad tonal color—like dialing in high-end air on a vocal or brightening a dull acoustic guitar.
expert_quote.author: Al Schmitt

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: A high-shelf filter boosts or cuts all frequencies uniformly above its corner frequency, ideal for adding air or taming harshness.

"Shelving EQs are great for adding broad tonal color—like dialing in high-end air on a vocal or brightening a dull acoustic guitar."
- Al Schmitt

questions.title: Practical Task: Vocal Presence Frequency Slider
questions.content: Adjust the rotary frequency slider to dial in the standard vocal presence and articulation boost frequency in Hz.
questions.label: Vocal Presence Frequency
questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Boosting around 4–6 kHz enhances vocal presence and consonant clarity, helping a lead vocal cut through a dense mix.

expert_quote.text: 5 kHz is where the human ear is most sensitive to speech intelligibility. A gentle boost here brings the singer right into the room with you.
expert_quote.author: Bruce Swedien, Recording Engineer

questions.expert_explanation: Boosting around 4–6 kHz enhances vocal presence and consonant clarity, helping a lead vocal cut through a dense mix.

questions.title: Q7: Kick Drum Fundamental Weight (50 Hz – 80 Hz)
questions.content: Which frequency range provides the fundamental low-end punch and weight of an acoustic kick drum?
questions.expert_explanation: An acoustic kick drum gets its deep fundamental weight and chest punch between 50 Hz and 80 Hz.

expert_quote.text: On kick drums, find the fundamental around 60 Hz for weight, carve out the hollow boxiness at 350 Hz, and push 4 kHz for beater snap.
expert_quote.author: Chris Lord-Alge

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: An acoustic kick drum gets its deep fundamental weight and chest punch between 50 Hz and 80 Hz.

"On kick drums, find the fundamental around 60 Hz for weight, carve out the hollow boxiness at 350 Hz, and push 4 kHz for beater snap."
- Chris Lord-Alge

questions.title: Practical Listening: Mix Mud & Clarity A/B Comparison
questions.content: Listen to Audio A and Audio B. Audio B has been cleaned with EQ. Which problematic area was attenuated to remove the 'mud'?
options: Cut between 250 Hz and 400 Hz low-mids
Cut between 2 kHz and 4 kHz upper-mids
questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Excessive energy between 250 Hz and 400 Hz creates boxiness and low-mid mud. Attenuating this region makes the mix sound cleaner and clearer.

expert_quote.text: Before you boost treble to add clarity, always clean out 300 Hz. Great mixing is subtractive first.
expert_quote.author: Bob Clearmountain, Mix Engineer

questions.correct_option: Cut between 250 Hz and 400 Hz low-mids
questions.expert_explanation: Excessive energy between 250 Hz and 400 Hz creates boxiness and low-mid mud. Attenuating this region makes the mix sound cleaner and clearer.

questions.title: Q9: Stereo Panning Controls & Soundstage Placement
questions.content: What does a stereo pan control adjust on a mixer channel?

answers.text: Overall master volume of the channel
Amount of reverb sent to the track
Placement between left and right speakers
Balance between treble and bass tone

questions.expert_explanation: Stereo panning positions a track anywhere from hard left to hard right, creating a phantom centre when balanced equally between both speakers.

expert_quote.text: Contrast creates width. If everything is wide, nothing is wide.
expert_quote.author: Dave Pensado

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: Stereo panning positions a track anywhere from hard left to hard right, creating a phantom centre when balanced equally between both speakers.

"Contrast creates width. If everything is wide, nothing is wide."
- Dave Pensado

questions.title: Q10: Centre Panning Placement Conventions
questions.content: In professional stereo mixing, which core elements are traditionally placed dead centre?

answers.text: Stereo overheads, rhythm guitars, and pads
Kick drum, bass, snare, and lead vocal
Every instrument panned centre in mono

questions.expert_explanation: Placing the kick, bass, snare, and lead vocal dead centre anchors the mix spine evenly across both speakers and preserves mono power.

expert_quote.text: Anchor your low end and your primary vocal down the center line; that gives you a solid foundation so your guitars, synths, and reverbs can stretch wide to the edges.
expert_quote.author: Bob Clearmountain

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: Placing the kick, bass, snare, and lead vocal dead centre anchors the mix spine evenly across both speakers and preserves mono power.

"Anchor your low end and your primary vocal down the centre line; that gives you a solid foundation so your guitars, synths, and reverbs can stretch wide to the edges."
- Bob Clearmountain

items.title: Topic 6: EQ & Stereo (Part 2)
items.description: Mastery quiz covering the fundamentals of EQ & Stereo.

questions.title: Q11: Acoustic Frequency Masking in a Busy Mix
questions.content: In audio mixing, what is psychoacoustic 'frequency masking'?

answers.text: Out-of-phase audio cancels bass in mono
Louder sounds obscure quieter similar frequencies

questions.expert_explanation: Frequency masking happens when two instruments share the same frequency range and the louder sound masks the quieter one. Subtractive EQ carves space for each part.

expert_quote.text: Don't EQ an instrument in solo. EQ the track so it steps out of the way of other elements and clears room for the mix.
expert_quote.author: Al Schmitt

questions.title: Q12: Surgical Q Notch Filtering for Problem Frequencies
questions.content: An acoustic guitar has an annoying resonance at 350 Hz. How should you set the EQ to remove it surgically?

answers.text: Use a narrow bandwidth with a high Q factor
Use a wide bandwidth with a low Q factor
Use a gentle high-pass filter with low resonance
Use a broad low-shelf cut across the midrange

questions.expert_explanation: The Q (Quality) factor defines the bandwidth of an EQ filter (Bandwidth = Centre Frequency / Q). A high Q value (such as Q = 8 to 12) produces an extremely narrow 'surgical' notch that can attenuate or eliminate an unwanted resonant frequency (e.g. 347 Hz acoustic body resonance or 50/60 Hz electrical mains hum) without affecting adjacent musical frequencies. Conversely, low Q values (Q = 0.5 to 1.0) create broad, musical tone-shaping curves.

expert_quote.text: Use broad EQ curves when boosting to add musical tone, and narrow high-Q notches when cutting to fix problems.
expert_quote.author: Classic Mixing Rule

questions.title: Q13: Phantom Centre Acoustic Illusion in Stereo Monitoring
questions.content: What is the 'phantom centre' in stereo monitoring?

answers.text: An acoustic null in an untreated room
A sound appearing directly between two speakers
A physical third speaker placed in the middle
Stereo reverb spread evenly across tracks

questions.expert_explanation: When both left and right speakers play an identical signal at equal volume, the listener perceives a phantom centre coming directly from between the speakers.

expert_quote.text: Contrast creates width. If everything is wide, nothing is wide. The phantom center anchors your mix.
expert_quote.author: Dave Pensado

questions.title: Q14: Stereo Panning Double-Tracked Guitars
questions.content: How are two separate takes of a rhythm guitar part typically panned to create a wide stereo rock mix?

answers.text: Both takes panned dead centre in mono
Low frequencies left and treble right
Routed into three separate delay buses
One take panned hard left, one hard right

questions.expert_explanation: Recording two distinct performances and panning them hard left and right creates natural stereo width without phase cancellation when summed to mono.
questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Recording two distinct performances and panning them hard left and right creates natural stereo width without phase cancellation when summed to mono.

questions.title: Q15: Stereo Pan Law Constant Volume Compensation
questions.content: Why do mixing consoles and DAWs use a 'Pan Law' (such as -3 dB or -4.5 dB)?

answers.text: Add analogue saturation on centre tracks
Compress loud peaks on wide-panned tracks
Keep perceived volume constant across panning
Prevent phase cancellation when checking mono

questions.expert_explanation: A Pan Law (typically -3 dB) attenuates signals panned to the centre so they do not sound louder when summed across both stereo speakers.

expert_quote.text: Without pan law, every instrument you pan toward the center will jump out in volume and clutter your mix balance.
expert_quote.author: Mixing Desk Principles

Expert Explanation: A Pan Law (typically -3 dB) attenuates signals panned to the centre so they do not sound louder when summed across both stereo speakers.

questions.title: Q16: Dynamic EQ vs Static Parametric EQ Processing
questions.content: How does a dynamic EQ differ from a standard static EQ?

answers.text: Static EQ only cuts; dynamic EQ only boosts
Dynamic EQ reacts to signal level above threshold
Dynamic EQ widens mono into stereo
Static EQ shifts the pitch of instruments

questions.expert_explanation: Unlike a static EQ’s fixed cut or boost, a dynamic EQ only attenuates or boosts a frequency band when the signal level crosses a set threshold.

expert_quote.text: Dynamic EQ is the ultimate scalpel because it only intervenes when a frequency misbehaves, leaving the natural tone untouched otherwise.
expert_quote.author: Tchad Blake

questions.title: Q17: Parametric EQ: Q and Bandwidth Control
questions.content: When cutting an annoying ringing frequency from a snare drum, how should the bandwidth (Q) be set?

answers.text: Wide bandwidth to boost overall brightness
Steep high-pass filter to cut low end
Narrow bandwidth (high Q) to isolate the ring
Zero gain setting to keep snare dynamics

questions.expert_explanation: A narrow bandwidth (high Q) lets you notch out an unwanted snare ring surgically without thinning out the rest of the drum’s tone.

expert_quote.text: Cut narrow to remove problems; boost broad to add musical character.
expert_quote.author: Bob Clearmountain, Mixing Engineer

questions.title: Q18: Complementary EQ (Kick Drum & Bass Guitar)
questions.content: When a kick drum and bass guitar clash in the low end, what is the standard EQ solution?

answers.text: Boost 60 Hz by +6 dB on both instruments
Pan kick hard left and bass hard right
Carve opposite frequencies so each has space

questions.expert_explanation: Complementary EQ gives each instrument its own pocket—for example, boosting kick thump at 60 Hz while dipping 60 Hz slightly on the bass guitar.
questions.explanation: Expert Explanation: Complementary EQ gives each instrument its own pocket—for example, boosting kick thump at 60 Hz while dipping 60 Hz slightly on the bass guitar.

questions.title: Q19: Mono Compatibility & Stereo Widening Phase Cancellation
questions.content: You apply a stereo widening plugin to a guitar track. Why does the guitar disappear when checked in mono?

answers.text: Heavy compression clamping peaks below threshold
Destructive phase cancellation between L and R

questions.expert_explanation: Artificial stereo wideners often invert phase or delay one side. When summed to mono, out-of-phase frequencies cancel out and the guitar vanishes.

expert_quote.text: Always check your mix in mono. A mix that sounds huge in stereo but collapses into hollow comb filtering in mono is a failed mix.
expert_quote.author: Michael Brauer

questions.title: Q20: Harmonic Pitch Calculation Across Octaves
questions.content: If concert pitch A4 vibrates at 440 Hz, what frequency is note A5 (one octave higher)?
questions.expert_explanation: Musical pitch follows a logarithmic frequency relationship where every octave step higher exactly doubles the fundamental frequency (fn = f0 * 2^n). Therefore, one octave above A4 (440 Hz) is A5 at 440 Hz * 2 = 880 Hz, while one octave below is A3 at 440 Hz / 2 = 220 Hz. Understanding octave math enables audio engineers to calculate musical harmonic intervals, set proportional filter bands, and surgically target resonant overtones.

expert_quote.text: The audio spectrum is fundamentally mathematical. If you know the root note of a song, you can calculate every resonant octave and harmonic overtone with precision.
expert_quote.author: Acoustic Theory Principles

items.title: Topic 7: FX & Processors (Part 1)
items.description: Core fundamentals of time-based and modulation effects: Delay time, Feedback, RT60 reverb decay, Pre-delay, Reverb types (Spring, Plate, Chamber), and Chorus & Flanging mechanics.

questions.title: Practical Listening: Delay FX Identification
questions.content: Listen to Audio A (Dry) and Audio B (Wet). What time-based effect has been added to the guitar in Audio B?
questions.explanation: Echo / Delay: Delay stores audio in a temporary buffer and reproduces discrete, audible repetitions delayed in time by milliseconds (ms) or tempo divisions (e.g., 1/4 note). The feedback parameter governs repetition decay.

expert_quote.text: Delay gives an instrument space and rhythm without washing it out like reverb does. It's the secret to deep, punchy mixes.
expert_quote.author: Tony Maserati, Mix Engineer (Beyoncé, Jay-Z)

questions.title: Q2: Delay Feedback Regeneration
questions.content: What does the 'Feedback' control adjust on a delay effect?

answers.text: The stereo width between the left and right delay repeats
The tone brightness of the repeats using an internal filter
The number of repeats by sending output back into input
The modulation speed of the delay time LFO sweep

questions.expert_explanation: Feedback (regeneration) routes a portion of the delayed output signal back into the processor input. At 0% feedback, only a single repeat (slapback) is heard. Higher feedback percentages generate progressively more decaying repeats until the energy dissipates.

expert_quote.text: Feedback is the memory loop of your delay. It dictates how long a musical idea lingers in the soundstage.
expert_quote.author: Time-Based FX Manual

Expert Explanation: Feedback (regeneration) routes a portion of the delayed output signal back into the processor input. At 0% feedback, only a single repeat (slapback) is heard. Higher feedback percentages generate progressively more decaying repeats until the energy dissipates.

questions.title: Practical Listening: Reverb Decay Identification
questions.content: Listen to Audio A (Dry) and Audio B (Wet). What acoustic effect has been added to create an illusion of space?
questions.explanation: Reverberation: Reverb simulates the acoustic reflections of a physical room, consisting of early reflections followed by a dense, decaying reverberant wash characterized by RT60 (reverberation time).

expert_quote.text: Reverb is the acoustic architecture of your song. It tells the listener where the band is standing in physical space.
expert_quote.author: Eddie Kramer, Engineer (Jimi Hendrix, Led Zeppelin)

questions.title: Q4: Reverb Pre-Delay (Initial Delay)
questions.content: Why is 'Pre-Delay' added to a reverb when mixing lead vocals?

answers.text: It shortens the total decay time of the reverb tail
It boosts the treble presence frequencies of the reverb reflections
It eliminates low-frequency mud by inverting the stereo reverb phase
It separates dry vocal transients from the reverb for better clarity

questions.expert_explanation: Pre-delay inserts an intentional silent gap (typically 20 to 60 ms) between the dry direct signal and the first reverberation reflections. This allows transient consonants to cut through clearly at the front of the mix before the reverb tail blooms.

expert_quote.text: Pre-delay is how you get a massive vocal reverb without pushing the singer into the back row of the concert hall.
expert_quote.author: Vocal Mixing Essentials

Expert Explanation: Pre-delay inserts an intentional silent gap (typically 20 to 60 ms) between the dry direct signal and the first reverberation reflections. This allows transient consonants to cut through clearly at the front of the mix before the reverb tail blooms.

questions.title: Q5: Reverb Types — Spring Reverb
questions.content: How does a traditional electromechanical spring reverb generate its sound?

answers.text: By vibrating a large suspended steel plate inside an iron frame
By passing an audio signal through physical coiled metal steel springs
By broadcasting sound into a tiled echo chamber with stereo microphones
By looping magnetic tape across multiple playback heads at varying speeds

questions.expert_explanation: Spring reverbs use an input transducer coil to send audio vibrations down one or more coiled steel springs suspended in a metal tank. A pickup coil at the other end converts the mechanical vibrations back into electrical signal, producing a distinctive bright, bouncy, metallic timbre.

expert_quote.text: Spring reverb defined the sound of surf rock, blues, and vintage guitar amplifiers like the Fender Twin Reverb.
expert_quote.author: Guitar Tech Reference

questions.explanation:
Expert Explanation: Spring reverbs use an input transducer coil to send audio vibrations down one or more coiled steel springs suspended in a metal tank. questions.title: Q6: Reverb Types — Plate Reverb
questions.content: What physical mechanism creates reverberation in a classic plate reverb (like an EMT 140)?

answers.text: A tiled room with a loudspeaker and two boundary microphones
Coiled metal springs vibrating inside a guitar combo amplifier chassis
A large suspended steel sheet vibrated by an audio transducer
An analogue bucket brigade chip delaying audio through internal capacitors

questions.expert_explanation: A plate reverb suspends a large, thin sheet of steel (approximately 1x2 metres) under high tension within a heavy outer frame. A driver transducer vibrates the centre of the sheet, and contact pickups capture the resulting dense, high-frequency reflections, making it the classic studio choice for vocals and snare drums.

expert_quote.text: Plate reverb lacks discrete early reflections, giving you immediate, shimmering diffusion that blends seamlessly behind vocals.
expert_quote.author: Vintage Studio Processing
